::: {.why}
The default model of the field, and the honest question is not whether it fits better in sample but whether the interactions it finds are real at this signal-to-noise ratio.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Tune a gradient boosting model under the frozen protocol and report its out-of-sample performance with an interval.
- Say what functional form a tree ensemble can represent that a linear model cannot, and test whether that form is present in your data.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Tune it properly with the purged splitter: depth, learning rate, subsample fraction and the number of rounds chosen by early stopping inside each fold. Report out-of-sample R-squared and information ratio with intervals, next to the linear baseline.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Test for the thing it is supposed to find: add the two-way interactions the tree model implies as explicit features to the linear model and see whether the linear model closes the gap. If it does, the boosting gain is a functional form you can name; if it does not, the gain is either nonlinearity you have not characterised or overfitting.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A tuned boosting model with intervals, plus the interaction test showing whether a linear model with named interactions closes the gap.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Your boosting model beats ridge by 15 percent in cross-validated R-squared. Give three explanations and say how you would distinguish them.
:::
